The Epomaker HE75 V2 TMR is a keyboard that knows what it is. It provides TMR switches, a hurtling-fast polling rate, and a small build at a price just under its competition. It's not particularly flashy, and it has no gimmick, but it's just a solid, solid competitive keyboard, and one you can fit in your backpack.

PC Gamer's got your back Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you. Find out more about how we evaluate games and hardware.

It feels like every new bit of tech in a gaming keyboard or gaming mouse is treated as the next frontier, from new switch types to higher polling rates, and even the materials used. But if you want 8,000 Hz polling, it actually does feel like TMR might be the next frontier, because not only is it snappy and responsive, but it's super efficient, which helps counteract some of the problems with high polling in the first place.

Right now, the pickings are fairly slim for TMR keyboards. We've got some from Logitech, some from Cherry, and a few others, but it's still a relatively niche sensor technology for switches right now, and not exactly cheap. But TMR is great, and it's particularly good if you want to go wireless thanks to its power efficiency.

Epomaker's HE75 V2 TMR is interesting partly because it crams that switch technology into an 8,000 Hz board with a ton of little quality-of-life features, and does it all at a price point amongst the cheapest TMR keyboards. But whether it's worth the asking fee will come down to feel and play.

✅ You want a compact competitive keeb: It might not look it, but the HE75 V2 TMR is a beast in the specs department, and it fits that into an ickle frame.

❌ You don't care about TMR switches or high polling: If you can make do with Hall effect or plain 'ol mechanical switches, you can get a keyboard for cheaper, or one loaded with more features.

The Epomaker HE75 V2 TMR is a keyboard that knows what it is. It provides TMR switches, a hurtling-fast polling rate, and a small build at a price just under its competition. It's not particularly flashy, and it has no gimmick, but it's just a solid, solid competitive keyboard, and one you can fit in your backpack.

Epomaker Creamy Jade Magnetic Switch (pre-lubed)

Yes, with magnetic and 3 / 5-pin mechanical switches.

Wired and wireless (2.4 GHz and Bluetooth)

Dynamic RGB per-key backlight and adjustable front light

60 hours with RGB off and 33.5 with RGB on (8,000 Hz)

8,000 Hz polling is far more than the average gamer needs (myself included), and it's even paired with the likes of rapid trigger, making this a super competitive keyboard in the specs department. You aren't getting a wrist rest or many extras here, but it does come with a five-layer sound-dampening gasket, one media dial, and my model came with pre-lubed Creamy Jade Magnetic switches.

TMR and Hall effect are both contactless magnetic sensor-based systems, though they are different terms, which does make the HE in the name confusing. The standard HE75 is Hall effect, hence the name, so this V2 model is the TMR version of a Hall effect keyboard. Understood? Great.

The broader benefit of TMR switches is that they are uber precise, detecting changes of 0.01 mm, and because they measure resistance (rather than a constant voltage), they use less power than the likes of Hall effect. That makes them especially good for wireless peripherals that rely on battery power, like this one (though you can also keep it plugged in).

They also have the same benefit as Hall effect switches in that no physical contact happens; therefore, there's no wear. This is perhaps more of a benefit in controllers that can get drift. They are more or less a straight upgrade from Hall effect, hence the recent adoption in the gaming market.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

The HE 75 V2 TMR (unlike the standard HE 75 V2) is hot-swappable with magnetic or 3/5-pin mechanical switches.

I have come to love the size of this keyboard from my weeks with it. You get your standard keys, your F keys, an extra media dial, but not much else. It's a compact build that's sturdy, weighty, and not too heavy either.

There's only a little space between the number keys and F keys, and yet I rarely hit the wrong key. I can say the same for the arrow keys on the right. I could see one accidentally activating rapid trigger mode by hitting Fn and Shift together when trying to hit the right Shift, but I've never managed to do so in-game.

As for typing feel, the HE 75 V2 TMR is smooth and responsive. It's relatively clacky, which I find quite satisfying in use, and though keys are rather smushed together to fit on the board, the PBT keycaps are smooth to the touch and easy to press down.

Playing Terraria-like crafter Delverium, I notice almost no hand strain. This is less a competitive game and more one you'd play for hours in the evening, but it's important that a gaming keyboard can last for both a hardcore session and a cosy one. The only downside here is the lack of a wrist rest means you are reliant on the comfort of your tabletop to brace the weight of your arm. But the HE75 V2 TMR is accommodating to the palm, and despite being sturdy, it doesn't feel angular.

In Counter-Strike 2, it is super snappy. Given that you can set actuation anywhere between 0.1 mm and 3 mm, I found myself prioritising the WASD keys, and this feels natural in context. 8,000 Hz may be overkill, but I can say that, whether wired or wireless, the HE 75 V2 TMR is a competitive ol' beast. It's smooth, reactive, easy to press, and it's never hard to find my place on the board thanks to its accommodating size and angled shape.

The entire keyboard goes up ever so slightly at the top, which can then be pushed further up with its included feet. Rather handily, it hides away the 2.4 GHz connector under the right foot, which is a neat bit of storage.

Simplicity is the aim of the HE 75 VR TMR. My model is the black variant, and it comes with all-black keycaps with a white font. The only flashy element of the entire build is a strip of light in the back of the keyboard that is accompanied by a crystallised lining. You can customise this in the software to any colour, but it's much more noticeable for the streaks of light it produces on my mousepad than the look of the strip itself.

The HE 75 V2 TMR does have per-key RGB, and with the keys being somewhat opaque, it shines through well. To me, the keyboard looks solid with or without RGB, but it doesn't really stand out.

One thing I do like is that almost every aesthetic choice is also practical (barring the light bar). It has a small light on the bottom right, and this indicates whether you have turned rapid trigger on or off. The media dial on the top right is very low-key in its presentation, but functions well, and has enough space on the board to be easy to find.

Epomaker, unlike many peripheral manufacturers, pulls out a big win in the software department, as it's not only intuitive and easy to use, but can also be done entirely through a web page. You simply 'bind' your device to the tab (just find it via settings), then you can do custom button mapping, swap lighting, set actuation, and update software.

In my weeks using this keyboard every single day, I've not had a single software hiccup. And, other than getting updates or setting actuation, you can control a lot of the keyboard's software through a smart grouping of function key combinations.

Thanks perhaps to the 8,000 mAh battery, or the more efficient TMR switches, you can get up to 60 hours of battery life in 8,000 Hz mode with the RGB off and up to 33.5 with RGB on. Given 8,000 Hz polling seems to drain battery anywhere between five and seven times faster, I'd expect around 300 to 350 hours of battery on 1,000 Hz with RGB off, and just over half that figure with RGB on.

I'd consider that battery life solid, and more than enough to make the HE75 V2 TMR both good on the go and great in a wireless minimalist setup. The likes of the Keychron K8 Ultra 8K deliver up to 760 hours with RGB off, so you will get better battery from comparably priced keyboards, but 350 hours is enough that I'd be surprised if you charge it more than once every few months.

If you need to check the battery life, you simply hit FN and Space, and it shows the battery in RGB. It's a neat touch.

There's a deep thock to it, but one that doesn't reverberate.

The HE V2 TMR has a five-layer gasket designed for softer keystrokes, and though I wouldn't call the keyboard quiet, I would say it offers a fairly satisfying sound. There's a deep thock to it, but one that doesn't reverberate.

It's a deep, satisfying sound, especially so when you consider the top is a thick plastic. I was expecting a more shrill or generally more hollow sound, but the five layers give it some depth. I'd say it's fairly comparable to the TMR Cherry keyboard I tried earlier this year, the XTRFY MX 8.2 Pro TMR TKL.

It does have a slightly more weighty sound in the space bar and in the Enter switch, which I assume is partly related to them being bigger keys, but also partly with the space bar not being surrounded by keycaps. Though they sound different, none sound bad.

As far as TMR boards are concerned, this is a very good price. The Cherry K5 Pro TMR Compact is a smaller board and costs more. The MX 8.2 Pro TMR TKL is over $100 more. You are getting more keys here, and I think the Pro TMR TKL has a stronger base, but I'd easily pick the Epomaker if it were my money.

But if you don't need a TMR keyboard, there are plenty of cheaper options. Gamakay's X NaughShark NS68 goes all the way down to just $40, and it comes with Hall effect switches. It's missing a media dial and dedicated F keys, but it's a relatively similar size. The Epomaker, however, blows it out of the shark-infested waters where build quality is concerned. The HE75 V2 TMR really does feel like a $130 keyboard to my fingertips.

I think the questions you have to ask yourself if you're thinking about the Epomaker HE75 V2 TMR are: 'How important are TMR switches to you?', 'Do I need 8K?', 'Will I need a numpad or wrist rest?' and 'Do I want something flashier?'. If the answers to those questions are yes, yes, no and no, then I'd say the HE75 V2 TMR is a bit of a winner.

The HE75 V2 TMR is strongly built, with a solid feature set, and it balances a small size with a solid offering of keys. I found myself pleasantly surprised by the amount of desk space left after the V2 TMR took over full-time, and I've never found myself lacking in competitive matches either. Well, any more than I usually am.

#3819. Nintendo says it isn't planning any more Switch 2 price hikes

Nintendo, which unveiled the results of the first half of its fiscal year 2027 earlier today, has now said it has access to enough quantities of memory to manufacture more Switch 2 consoles.

As a result, the platform holder does not plan to increase the price of the Switch 2. That's according to Reuters, citing Nintendo president Shuntaro Furukawa.

Nintendo, which has so far sold 26m Switch 2 consoles, has already raised the price of the console earlier this year. The price hikes, which took effect on 1st September in the US, Canada, Japan and Europe, saw the console's price increase by $50 / €30 / ¥10,000. Although that was technically the first price hike for the console itself, prior to the Switch 2's launch last year, Nintendo raised the price of Switch 2 accessories in the US as a result of the Trump Administration's tariffs.

The reason that would cause Nintendo to raise prices again is the same that already caused rival PlayStation and Xbox to do so: AI-driven, global memory and storage shortages.

PlayStation already raised PS5 and PS5 Pro prices, on several occasions. Xbox has likewise gone through multiple rounds of price hikes for its Series X and Series S consoles, with the most recent having taken place in August.

That same crisis pushed one of Nintendo's longtime ROM suppliers to exit the business, opting instead to focus on the more lucrative business segments. ROM memory is used in Switch cartridges, though Nintendo hasn't commented on the news.

Incidentally, Switch 2 hardware sales have been in decline for several quarters now compared to its banner launch in 2025. Still, Switch 2 sales are tracking ahead of the Switch 1.

#3818. My Favorite Travel Headphones Are $250 Off Right Now

As a headphone reviewer, not many headphones outside of the flagship Sony, Bose, and Apple models get me excited. However, the JBL Tour One M3 Smart Tx headphones became the exception to that rule when I started using them over my Sony 1000XM6 as my go-to headphones. And right now, the Tour One M3s are down to $199.95 (originally $449.95), their lowest price ever, according to price-tracking tools. This is a great deal for these headphones, which I deemed my favorite travel headphones in my review.

Everything from design to the features on the Tour One M3 was made with travel in mind. The headphones are very light, which, along with the comfortable soft earcups and headband, makes them great for wearing for long periods of time. I was able to wear these on a long flight without feeling any discomfort. Feeling like you're not wearing any headphones is the gold standard for comfort, and the Tour One M3 nails that aspect. The battery life is also impressive, with up to 70 hours with ANC off and 40 hours with it on.

The travel case is compact, convenient, and has extra storage for the audio transmitter, which is the best feature of the Tour One M3. This is a high-quality, low-latency audio transmitter. Anything that you can plug an AUX cable, USB, or USB-C port into can stream high-quality, 24-bit audio wirelessly to the Tour One M3. The main way most people will use these headphones is by plugging them into the in-flight entertainment, which lets you watch movies in high-quality LDAC with ANC. But I've also been able to use them to watch TV.

The Tour One M3 Smart Tx are incredible traveling headphones, especially at $199.95, and I recommend them to anyone who values comfort, battery life, simplicity, and likes the idea of the audio transmitter.

A lot of attention has been focused on the "Save Mass Effect" petition on Change.org, which has now drawn over 300,000 signatures collectively calling on Electronic Arts to make a new Mass Effect game.

But there's another petition in the works, asking the government of Canada to save BioWare—the people, not the product—and while it only has a tiny fraction of names attached to it, it's enough that the Canadian government will actually have to look at it.

Unlike the Change.org petition, this one is official, in that it's actually part of the legislative process: Public petitions like e-7989, as it's formally known, are "used to draw attention to an issue of public concern. They ask the House of Commons, the Government of Canada, a minister or a member to take or refrain from taking some action."

The requested actions in this case are three:

As I write this, the petition is nosing toward 3,000 signatures, not a huge amount but enough to trigger the next step in the process. Once an electronic petition has at least 500 valid signatures—that is, the signature of a Canadian citizen or resident—it's certified, at which point the Member of Parliament representing the petitioner can either present it during Routine Proceedings, or file it with the Clerk of the House.

There are various other rules and norms in place, but the important bit is that "the government must respond to every petition presented to the House within 45 calendar days of its presentation or filing with the Clerk." Electronic petitions can be short-circuited by the dissolution of Parliament: Paper petitions can be re-presented to the House even if they were certified by a previous Parliament, but electronic petitions are wiped and must be restarted afresh.

The good news for committed videogame optimists is that, for many reasons, the current Canadian Parliament is not going to be dissolved anytime soon, so this petition to free BioWare from the fetters of EA isn't going to just die on the vine. But, also for a variety of reasons, it's not liable to lead to BioWare's salvation, either.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

For one thing, while New Democratic Party leader Avi Lewis expressed support for the idea of government intervention shortly after BioWare was closed by its new owners, the NDP is not in power right now and its attention is currently consumed by rebuilding after a decade of disastrous leadership. The government of Canada is also focused on other things at the moment, for instance the badly frayed relationship with our erratic, nuclear-tipped neighbor to the south, and while cheerleading companies like BioWare is great PR (and the current governing party loves that stuff), it's not something that's likely to inspire actual action.

Maybe the most salient roadblock is this: BioWare and its games are owned by Electronic Arts, which has shown no interest in selling them off. Even if the government of Canada were interested in floating BioWare the cash to go independent, it can't buy what EA's not selling—and historically, EA has not made a habit of letting go of its properties.

This is a pattern with videogame publishers like EA. They buy smaller developers, set unrealistic timelines, overwork their employees, and meddle in the development process, resulting in poorer quality games. Then, when sales fail to meet expectations, they blame the developers, lay off workers, and eventually shut down the studio for short-term profit.

Still, the NDP is taking the matter seriously. "BioWare has cultivated an international following from their renowned videogame franchises like Mass Effect, Baldur’s Gate, and Dragon Age. Canada’s videogame industry creates some of our most important cultural exports, and BioWare was among our biggest success stories," MP Don Davies, the sponsor of the petition, told PC Gamer.

"Electronic Arts, their American parent company, was never invested in the success of BioWare since they purchased the studio as part of a larger acquisition in 2007. This is a pattern with videogame publishers like EA. They buy smaller developers, set unrealistic timelines, overwork their employees, and meddle in the development process, resulting in poorer quality games. Then, when sales fail to meet expectations, they blame the developers, lay off workers, and eventually shut down the studio for short-term profit.

"New Democrats want BioWare to stay in business, preferably under Canadian control. We believe that the employees at BioWare ought to have the first opportunity to buy back their studio and continue making the games that fans love. The petition primarily asks the federal government to provide the required capital. This is absolutely possible. Our goal with the petition is to demonstrate just how many Canadians believe this is a worthwhile investment in our entertainment industry."

BioWare is an Edmonton-based video game studio that created acclaimed series like #MassEffect, Baldur’s Gate, and Dragon Age. Canada’s video game industry creates some of our most important cultural exports, and #BioWare is among our greatest success stories.

I do think it's something of a distant dream to expect the Canadian government to whip out the chequebook on this one, but that's not to say that this public petition is a waste of time. There's value in speaking out in support of good causes or opposition to bad ones, and this petition's focus on BioWare and its people, rather than just 'I want more Mass Effect,' makes it worth getting behind. At the very least, we get a final, formal vocalization of support for the people that gave us so many great memories.

And who knows? This has been a pretty good week for good things happening, after all—maybe there's still a little gas left in that tank.

The petition will be open for signatures until March 4, 2027. Add your name to the list at ourcommons.ca.

#3813. Remakes and new games "both have a place in the stable" says Nintendo boss, buoyed by the success of Star Fox and Ocarina of Time

It's been a good year for Nintendo: between Star Fox - the N64 classic with a dazzling facelift on Switch 2 - and the newly-launched and utterly fantastic Ocarina of Time remake, the platform holder is having a good run. And that's before you get to the likes of Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave, Nintendo Switch Sports Resort, Mario Tennis Fever or any of the Switch 2 re-releases of first-party Switch games, like Xenoblade Chronicles 3 or Animal Crossing: New Horizons.

As popular as its other games are, though, you have to admit that 2026 has been a banner year for Nintendo's remakes - both Star Fox and Ocarina of Time have commanded plenty of headline-grabbing attention over the past 12 months, and it's a fact that isn't lost on the company. In a new interview with Polygon, Nintendo's Nate Bihldorff - senior vice president of product development and publishing - says that wholly new games and remakes of classics are of "equal importance" to the publisher going forward.

"I do think that new games and remakes both have a place in the Nintendo stable, of equal importance to be honest," Bihldorff told the site at the Ocarina of Time's launch event in New York City. "There are fans of every single IP that we have out there. Of course, having new games in those series is wonderful, and I look forward to them as much as anyone else does, but there’s also a deep satisfaction in revisiting games that were very, very special, like Ocarina of Time… But it's also important to think about how many people had never played the original, and for them, the remake of Ocarina of Time is going to be an absolutely brand-new, 2026 experience, and one that I just cannot wait for them to get their hands on."

There's more interesting stuff in the interview, as Bihldorff outlines his views on the strenght of the Nintendo roster - "it doesn't matter how excited I am about Donkey Kong Bananza at launch; there's always going to be more games that are coming down the pipeline" - and that the release pipeline continues to look as strong for the Switch 2 as it did for the Switch. "There's one constant that has been consistent through my entire career at Nintendo, and that's that you can pretty much set your watch by the idea that we're going to be coming out with stuff," Bihldorff told Polygon.

Ocarina of Time is off to a very strong start; aside from being critically adored, the game has taken off virally - I can't move on my own feeds for clips of the game, people reminiscing about their original memories of certain locations, or long posts about the nostalgic elements of the title. Star Fox, meanwhile, has 1.17 million copies worldwide since its launch earlier this year on the Nintendo Switch 2, making it the ninth best-selling game on the platform (this is via Nintendo's financials yesterday). I expect Ocarina will outpace that.

Whatever your personal opinon on remakes in games, you cannot deny that it is a large part of the industry - and it seems Nintendo is keen to ride that wave as far as it'll go.

With all that said, when will I get my Pokemon Black and White remakes, then?
